implementation_notes: The BCL owns the pattern: System.Lazy<T> starts uninitialised and runs the factory on first access, and with LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication (the default thread-safe mode) exactly one factory run happens while other threads block and then see the published value; PublicationOnly allows several runs with only one published value, and LazyInitializer.EnsureInitialized(ref target, ref initialized, ref syncLock, factory) does the same for plain fields and structs without allocating a wrapper. It replaces the check-then-lock structure entirely, and the hand-written alternative (a volatile field plus lock plus repeated check) is only justified on .NET Framework code paths where the Lazy<T> wrapper is measurable in a hot loop. Writing the classic form without volatile is the documented bug: the CLI memory model allows the reference store to become visible before the object's fields.
pitfalls: Lazy<T> is single-shot and per instance: PublicationOnly can run the factory several times and may publish a value whose factory threw elsewhere, which leaks unmanaged resources allocated by the losing runs.
Touching Value from inside the factory throws InvalidOperationException (the built-in recursion detection), so an initialiser must not reference the lazy cell it is building.

The hand-rolled variant must be volatile-aware and lock on a private object: locking on this, a Type or a string risks external deadlock, and a non-volatile field reorders the publication on ARM64 and under some JIT optimisations.
Lazy<T> hides exceptions in a cached fault (ExecutionAndPublication caches the exception for every caller), so a transient failure needs an explicit retry above the Lazy<T> rather than inside it.
